## Robustness Assessment
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

Robustness depends on whether nearby changes in feature specification, reward
definition, transaction-cost assumptions, or split design materially alter the
conclusions for the high-frequency TD3 setup. Stable results indicate structural
effects; unstable results suggest dependence on a narrow experimental design.

```{python}
#| label: robustness_setup
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd

from thesis_mlflow_results import audit_plots_enabled, load_experiment_snapshot, runs_overview_table, show_table_meta

EXPERIMENT_NAME = "pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected_dsr"
snapshot = load_experiment_snapshot(EXPERIMENT_NAME)
finished = snapshot.latest_finished
runs_df = runs_overview_table(EXPERIMENT_NAME)
_audit = audit_plots_enabled()
```


## Hypothesis 2: Transaction-Cost Sensitivity {#sec-h2-transaction-cost-sensitivity}
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

This section varies the proportional transaction cost while holding the
algorithm, feature set, and reward fixed, on a baseline with the selected
10-feature set, log-return reward, and zero fee. It serves two purposes: it
locates the fee level at which the learned edge disappears, and it is the
decisive test of the reworded Hypothesis 1.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-h2-transaction-costs
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Hypothesis 2 transaction-cost sensitivity: test-split metrics across fee levels."

import pandas as pd
from thesis_mlflow_results import load_scenario_metrics
from thesis_tables import fmt_val, display_df, table_note

_SENS_COLS = [
    ("sharpe_ratio",  "Sharpe",   ".3f"),
    ("sortino_ratio", "Sortino",  ".3f"),
    ("total_return",  "Return",   ".2e"),
    ("max_drawdown",  "Max DD",   ".2e"),
    ("win_rate",      "Win Rate", ".2%"),
    ("profit_factor", "PF",       ".3f"),
    ("turnover",      "Turnover", ".4f"),
]

# The 0 bp arm is a clone of the H1 configuration (same features, reward,
# train_size), differing only by env.trading_fees, so the ladder is a
# single-factor sweep at a matched training budget. It is a separate training
# run from Chapter 6.1's own TD3 agent, not the same checkpoint re-priced.
_fees_scenarios = [
    ("pooled_td3_h2_fees_0_dsr",   "0 bp"),
    ("pooled_td3_h2_fees_1e6_dsr", "0.01 bp"),
    ("pooled_td3_h2_fees_1e5_dsr", "0.1 bp"),
    ("pooled_td3_h2_fees_1e4_dsr", "1 bp"),
]

rows = []
for exp, label in _fees_scenarios:
    m = load_scenario_metrics(exp)
    row = {"Fees": label}
    for key, col, fmt in _SENS_COLS:
        row[col] = fmt_val(m.get(key), fmt)
    rows.append(row)
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

if df.iloc[:, 1:].isin(["—"]).all().all():
    print("No results yet. Run: uv run thesis-experiments h2")
else:
    display_df(df)
    table_note(source="Author's own calculations.")
    show_table_meta(finished, audit=_audit)
```

The transaction-cost comparison is where the reworded Hypothesis 1 is decided.
Hypothesis 1 claims the learned edge is real but of the same order of magnitude
as the cost of trading on it, and the fee sweep tests exactly that. The policy
trades actively at 0 and 0.01 basis points; turnover collapses to essentially
zero at 0.1 and 1 basis points, and cumulative return follows the same break.
This is a per-trade cost of a few hundredths to a few tenths of a basis
point, which is the scale of the bid–ask half-spread on these instruments. The
half-spread is the maximum edge the microstructure feature set can express
(Section 4.3, @sec-execution-model-signal-friction). The fee sweep and the
half-spread bound therefore locate the learned edge from opposite directions: it
is positive but approximately one half-spread per trade, captured under
frictionless execution and eliminated by realistic spread-crossing cost. That is
the evidential content of Hypothesis 1 as reworded.

The break between 0.01 and 0.1 basis points is not just a sign flip in the
reported return; it is the point at which the policy stops trading altogether,
which admits a more direct mechanical explanation. The minimum price increment
for these instruments is one cent, so the smallest possible move in the
mid-price, when only one side of the book updates, is half a cent. At the mean
price of each instrument over the evaluation window this sets a break-even fee
-- the proportional cost at which a one-sided minimum-tick move stops covering
the fee -- ranging from roughly 0.08 basis points for the highest-priced
instrument to roughly 0.24 basis points for the lowest-priced one
(@tbl-tick-breakeven-fee). The observed break sits below every one of these
break-even points, which is consistent with Section 4.3's framing of the
half-spread as a ceiling on the expressible edge rather than the edge the agent
actually realizes on a given trade: the policy stops scalping before the fee
mathematically exceeds the largest possible tick-driven move, not only after.
This is a plausible reading of the current fee-ladder run, not a confirmed
mechanism, and the per-instrument breakdown does not fully support it. If the
break-even fee were set independently per instrument, turnover should collapse
first for the highest-priced instruments and last for the lowest-priced ones.
Instead, turnover collapses to zero for all six instruments simultaneously,
between the same two fee levels. This is consistent with how the policy is
trained: one network is shared across all six instruments, and the input
features are z-score normalized per symbol before the policy ever sees them, so
the model has no access to an instrument's absolute price level and cannot
condition its trading threshold on it. The tick-size arithmetic explains why a
break exists somewhere in this fee range at all; it does not explain, and on
this evidence cannot explain, why the six instruments break together rather
than in sequence.

For Hypothesis 2 itself, the same table carries a distinct conclusion: empirical
performance is materially sensitive to the transaction-cost assumption (a
parameter often left implicit). The fact that the sign changes within one
order of magnitude of fee is why robustness analysis is a precondition for any
economic claim here. Hypothesis 1 says how large the edge is; Hypothesis 2 says
how fast the reported result moves when this assumption is varied.

## Hypothesis 3: Feature Specification Sensitivity
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

This section compares three feature-specification levels under otherwise
identical conditions (same algorithm, data, reward, and transaction cost) to
assess whether richer microstructure-aware state representations improve
out-of-sample performance.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\begin{landscape}
```
:::

```{python}
#| label: h3_feature_comparison
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Hypothesis 3 feature sensitivity: test-split metrics for minimal (3), selected (10), and full (33) feature sets."

from thesis_tables import build_comparison_rows, comparison_table_html

_FEATURE_SCENARIOS = [
    ("pooled_td3_h3_features_minimal",                           "Minimal (3 features)",   False),
    ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected", "Selected (10 features)", True),
    ("pooled_td3_h3_features_full",                              "Full (33 features)",     False),
]

_FEATURE_COLS = [
    ("sharpe_ratio",          "Sharpe",   ".3f"),
    ("sortino_ratio",         "Sortino",  ".3f"),
    ("total_return",          "Return",   ".2e"),
    ("max_drawdown",          "Max DD",   ".2e"),
    ("win_rate",              "Win Rate", ".2%"),
    ("profit_factor",         "PF",       ".3f"),
    ("turnover",              "Turnover", ".4f"),
    ("annualized_volatility", "Ann. Vol", ".3f"),
]

_HIGHER_BETTER = {
    "sharpe_ratio": True, "sortino_ratio": True, "total_return": True,
    "max_drawdown": False, "win_rate": True, "profit_factor": True, "annualized_volatility": False,
}

scenario_metrics = [(label, load_scenario_metrics(exp), is_base) for exp, label, is_base in _FEATURE_SCENARIOS]
rows = build_comparison_rows(scenario_metrics, _FEATURE_COLS, index_col="Feature Set", higher_better=_HIGHER_BETTER)

if all(row.get("Sharpe", "—") == "—" for row in rows):
    print("No Hypothesis 3 results available. Run: uv run thesis-experiments h3")
else:
    display(comparison_table_html(rows, _FEATURE_COLS, index_col="Feature Set"))
    show_table_meta(finished, audit=_audit)
```

::: {.table-note}
**Source:** Author's own calculations.
**Legend:** Sharpe: mean excess return / std (not annualized). Sortino: mean excess return / downside deviation (not annualized). Return: cumulative simple return. Max DD: maximum drawdown. Win Rate: fraction of positive-return steps. PF: profit factor (gross wins / gross losses). Turnover: mean absolute position change per step. Ann. Vol: annualized volatility.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\end{landscape}
```
:::

The feature comparison supports a qualified version of Hypothesis 3. The minimal
three-feature representation produces a negative cumulative return
($-3.45 \times 10^{-8}$), a profit factor below one, and a short-biased policy
that spends 77.2% of the evaluation window short. The selected 10-feature
microstructure representation improves the result to a positive cumulative
return ($1.29 \times 10^{-7}$), a profit factor of 2.01, and a materially
stronger Sortino ratio under the same data and evaluation protocol.

The full 33-feature representation does not improve further. It remains
positive on cumulative return ($2.68 \times 10^{-8}$), but underperforms the
selected representation on return, drawdown, profit factor, and turnover. This
suggests that the benefit comes from adding relevant microstructure information,
not from maximizing feature count. For this thesis, Hypothesis 3 is therefore supported
for the transition from a minimal snapshot representation to the selected
microstructure-aware state, but not for the claim that every broader feature set
is better.

## Hypothesis 4: Reward Function Design
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

This section compares the log-return baseline against the Differential Sharpe
Ratio reward on an otherwise identical configuration (selected 10-feature set,
zero transaction cost), holding the algorithm and data fixed.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-h4-reward-design
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Hypothesis 4 reward-design sensitivity: test-split metrics for log-return vs. Differential Sharpe Ratio."

_reward_scenarios = [
    ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected",     "Log Return (baseline)"),
    ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected_dsr", "Differential Sharpe (DSR)"),
]

rows = []
for exp, label in _reward_scenarios:
    m = load_scenario_metrics(exp)
    row = {"Variant": label}
    for key, col, fmt in _SENS_COLS:
        row[col] = fmt_val(m.get(key), fmt)
    rows.append(row)
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

if df.iloc[:, 1:].isin(["—"]).all().all():
    print("No results yet. Run: uv run thesis-experiments h4")
else:
    display_df(df)
    table_note(source="Author's own calculations.")
    show_table_meta(finished, audit=_audit)
```

The reward-design comparison shows that Differential Sharpe Ratio optimization
changes the learned policy in an economically meaningful direction. Relative to
the log-return baseline, the DSR run increases cumulative return from
$1.29 \times 10^{-7}$ to $2.28 \times 10^{-7}$, improves profit factor from
2.01 to 5.70, and reduces maximum drawdown from $-1.93 \times 10^{-7}$ to
$-1.05 \times 10^{-7}$. The DSR policy is also more balanced in exposure,
moving from an 86.7% long policy under log-return reward to an approximately
neutral 49.8% long and 50.2% short distribution. This supports Hypothesis 4:
the reward objective materially affects both performance and policy behavior.

Overall, the robustness evidence is strongest for transaction-cost sensitivity,
feature specification, and reward-design sensitivity. It is not yet strong
evidence of robustness across market regimes, longer samples, alternative
chronological splits, or repeated random seeds.

Seed-level robustness was spot-checked outside the formal hypotheses: a small
number of independent short-budget TD3 trials with different random seeds, using
the baseline configuration, were run to confirm that the reported performance
reflects systematic learning rather than a single favourable initialisation. A
full multi-seed study at the training budget used in the main experiments was
not carried out, so single-run variance remains a limitation (Section 6.1;
@sec-execution-realism).
